catalog_quote: We assume that Wala has stress accent (Hyman, 2006:231), and that each lexical word should have one syllable which is stressed. We also assume that stress is not lexically assigned. That is, it should in principle be predictable given the written form of a word. [p. 7] ... A concise description of stress assignment is possible if syllables are treated as being either heavy (shape (C)VV) or light (shape (C)V). We also refer to closed syllables in the spoken language as heavy. If the written word consists of two light syllables, then stress falls on the first syllable. ... In words consisting of three light syllables, stress also falls on the first syllable, with optional reduction of non-stressed syllables. ... Stress is assigned to all heavy syllables, but processes subsequent to stress assignment may produce surface forms containing heavy (viz. CVC), unstressed syllables. In two- and three-syllable words where the first syllable is heavy, that syllable bears stress. [p. 8] ... In words with written form CVCVV…, stress placement either depends on the word, or is variable (we are not sure which). ... Three other words in the recording show stress on second syllables that are heavy. ... The general procedure for assigning stress can be characterized as follows. Starting from the left edge of the word, form bimoraic feet. ... Assign primary stress to the leftmost foot. [p. 9]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable, not lexical. Syllables are light (C)V or heavy (C)VV / closed; from the left edge the word is parsed into bimoraic feet (a heavy syllable forms a foot alone, two lights pair up), the first syllable of every foot is stressed, and primary stress goes to the leftmost foot. In practice this puts primary stress on the first syllable of virtually every word, whether that syllable is light (tala 'path' [ˈtalɐ], olisi 'answer' [ˈɔlisɪ]) or heavy (daulu '3PC' [ˈdaʊlʊ]); the weight sensitivity shows in foot structure and secondary stresses and in a few CVCVV / 'a-initial words where a heavy second syllable takes primary stress ('amiu [ʔaˈmiu], 'adaoro 'kneel' [ʔaˈdaɔrɔ]). The authors call this an initial hypothesis from a single 2-minute 2011 recording; the catalog could equally file it as default-initial.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: the first syllable of each non-initial bimoraic foot carries secondary stress (kwairanai 'helping' (kwai)ra(nai) [ˈkpiːraˌneɪ]; fafu'isinai 'at last' (fafu)('isi)(nai) [ˈɸaɸˌʔisˌnaɪ]); secondary-stressed syllables are longer, may be louder, with low level pitch, vs primary = longer, louder, high level or high-falling pitch (p. 7). Fn. 3 p. 8: the authors are 'not confident in our ability to hear the difference between primary and secondary stress'; working hypothesis is that the leftmost foot is most prominent.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Words of shape CVCVV..: 'stress placement either depends on the word, or is variable (we are not sure which)' (p. 9) -- rerei, falua initial vs 'amiu, fa-meulu, ta~tae-na-la, 'adaoro with stress on a heavy second syllable, in each of which the first syllable is arguably a separate morph ('a-, dative fa-, reduplicant). (ii) The 1960 Capell recording 'has trisyllabic words consisting of three light syllables, where the second syllable is stressed', contrary to the 2011-based analysis (p. 5). (iii) Unstressed vowels may drop, leaving surface CVC unstressed syllables -- rules are 'opaque' (p. 8). (iv) Particles: locative 'i atonic; plural gi always stressed (lengthened when NP-final); definite article li stressed or unstressed (p. 10).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (lexical word plus tonic/atonic particles), analysed from connected read speech (John 1:19-28 read by one speaker, 2011) and Capell's 1960 recited texts; not citation forms; no consultant access. The bulk of the grammar rests on the written 2007 New Testament, so the phonology chapter is explicitly tentative.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the Wala of west-central Malaita (= Langalanga; ISO lgl, Glottolog wala1266); the grammar notes that dialect information is unavailable (p. 1) and that the 2011 recording is of a speaker from Guaidalo village (p. 5). Glottolog's third reference, Salomon 1953 'Grammaire de la langue de Wala: Mallicolo, Nouvelles Hébrides' (OCLC 225692251), by its own title describes Wala island off Malekula, Vanuatu, not Malaitan Wala; its [lgl] assignment in Glottolog appears to be a homonym error (the Malekula variety belongs to the Uripiv-Wala-Rano-Atchin language, Glottolog urip1239 -- my identification from the title, not verified by opening the work).
